steps.body: Every normal curve keeps the same promise, whatever its center μ and width σ: about 68% of values land within one σ of μ, about 95% within two, about 99.7% within three. Scores on a test with μ = 100, σ = 10 will be our running example.

widget.prompt: What percent of scores land between 90 and 110 — within one σ of the mean?
widget.lowFeedback: More than that — one σ each side already captures the bell's thick middle.
widget.highFeedback: Less than that — plenty of the curve still lies beyond one σ.
widget.successFeedback: About 68% — just over two-thirds live within one σ. That number is worth memorizing; the bell repeats it everywhere.

predict.prompt: Within ONE σ of the mean (90–110): more or less than half the scores?

options.label: More than half — the middle is where the bell is fat
Less than half — one σ is a narrow slice

predict.reveal: The bell piles most of its area in the middle: one σ each side holds about 68% — over two-thirds. Half would be a flat distribution's answer; the bell is anything but flat.

widget.prompt: What percent of scores land between 80 and 120 (within two σ)?

commonErrors.feedback: 68% is the ONE-σ share. Two σ each side captures more: 95%.
99.7% is the three-σ share. Two σ gives 95%.

widget.successFeedback: 95% within two σ — the interval behind every 'margin of error' you've met in this course.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Work from the memorized bell numbers: 68 within one σ, 95 within two, 99.7 within three — then halve for a single tail.

explanationVariants: Two σ each side of the mean captures 95% — the same 95% that margin-of-error intervals promise.
From 80 to 120 is μ ± 2σ; the empirical rule prices that band at 95% for every normal curve.

widget.prompt: What percent of scores land ABOVE 120?

commonErrors.feedback: 5% is BOTH tails together. Above 120 is only the right tail: half of 5%.
95% is INSIDE two σ. Above 120 is one tail of the remaining 5%.

widget.successFeedback: Outside two σ lives 5%, split evenly by symmetry: 2.5% in each tail.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Work from the memorized bell numbers: 68 within one σ, 95 within two, 99.7 within three — then halve for a single tail.

explanationVariants: Outside two σ lies 5%, and symmetry splits it: 2.5% above 120, 2.5% below 80.
One tail is always half of what both tails hold — halving is the bell's free bonus rule.

steps.body: Notice what just happened: symmetry let you split the leftover. Outside two σ is 5%; each tail takes exactly half. Every region under the bell is reachable from the three memorized numbers plus halving.

widget.prompt: What percent of scores land between 110 and 120?

commonErrors.feedback: 27% is BOTH bands (90→80 and 110→120... careful: the two flanks between one and two σ). One side takes half: 13.5%.

widget.successFeedback: From 68 to 95 the bell adds 27 points — split across two symmetric bands: 13.5% each side. You just did normal-curve arithmetic with no calculus in sight.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Work from the memorized bell numbers: 68 within one σ, 95 within two, 99.7 within three — then halve for a single tail.

explanationVariants: Between one and two σ the bell adds 95 − 68 = 27 points, shared by two symmetric bands: 13.5% each.
Any band's share comes from subtracting the memorized levels and halving by symmetry.
hints: The 110–120 band is the gap between the one-σ and two-σ fences on ONE side.
Within two σ is 95%; within one σ is 68%. The difference, 27%, is split across both flanks.
Half of 27: the right flank alone holds 13.5%.

widget.prompt: What percent of scores land beyond 130 or below 70 — outside three σ?

commonErrors.feedback: 99.7% is INSIDE three σ. Outside is what's left: 0.3%.
Careful with the decimal: 100 − 99.7 leaves 0.3%, not 3%.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Inside three σ holds 99.7% — outside is the leftover 0.3%.
widget.successFeedback: 0.3% — three-σ events are once-in-333 rarities. That's why chapter 4 treats them as near-proof.

explanationVariants: 99.7% within three σ leaves 0.3% outside — split across two tails, 0.15% each.
Three-σ events are the bell's outer country: rare enough that chapter 4 treats them as strong evidence.

steps.body: 68 – 95 – 99.7, then halve tails by symmetry. With μ and σ you can price any region of a normal world. Next: a ruler that measures distance in σ's directly.
takeaways: 68 – 95 – 99.7: the shares within one, two, three σ of the mean, for every normal curve.
Symmetry halves anything: one tail is half of what both tails hold.
Any band's share comes from subtracting memorized levels — no new facts needed.
steps.teaser: Next: a ruler that measures every distance in σ's directly — the z-score.
